title: Depression: a setback and the loop that follows
description: During a depressive episode, something goes wrong: a setback, or a painful thought about oneself. The episode follows what happens next: a stronger response to the bad news, a turn inward into going over it again and again, and difficulty leaving that loop. The typical response shows the same setback in a brain that is not depressed. Unlike the other states, this one does not start from a neutral baseline: some differences are already there at rest.
caveat: Depression is not a spike but a state lasting weeks or months, and no scan has followed a ruminating brain through a loop over minutes or hours. What the research gives is separate snapshots: how the depressed brain differs at rest, how it responds to negative pictures and to rewards, and which regions are active when healthy volunteers are asked to ruminate. Stitching these into "setback, then turning inward, then staying stuck" is a reconstruction, and the order of every step is inferred. The picture is also contested: one large pooled analysis of task studies found no consistent differences in task-related activity, with one small exception, and the largest study of resting connectivity found the default mode network less connected in depression, not more, mainly in people with recurrent depression and those on medication. Depression also varies widely between people.

phases.name: At rest
phases.caption: Before anything happens, there are already differences. The subgenual cingulate, deep in the front of the brain, is more active at rest, and in most studies it is more tightly linked to the network the brain uses for self-focused thought.
phases.typicalCaption: Before anything happens: an ordinary resting brain, active but in balance.

phases.name: A setback
phases.caption: Something goes wrong. The amygdala, insula and dorsal anterior cingulate respond more strongly to the bad news than in a brain that is not depressed, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a control region, responds less.
phases.typicalCaption: Something goes wrong. The amygdala and anterior cingulate respond, as they do to anything negative.

order.rationale: The studies compare the response to negative pictures with the response to neutral ones. Using that as "the moment of a setback" in a continuous episode is an inference.

phases.name: Turning inward
phases.caption: Attention turns inward, to going over what happened and what it says about oneself. The default mode network, the regions active in self-focused thought, comes forward, working closely with the subgenual cingulate.
phases.typicalCaption: A few moments of going over what happened. The same self-focused network is active here too; rumination is something every brain does.

order.rationale: That rumination follows a negative event is how rumination is defined, not something measured in a scanner. The regions come from studies in which healthy volunteers were asked to ruminate.

phases.name: Staying there
phases.timescale: minutes to hours, recurring over weeks
phases.caption: The loop is hard to leave, and comes round again. Meanwhile good things land more faintly: the striatum, part of the reward system, responds less when something goes well.
phases.typicalCaption: Attention returns to the outside world and the brain settles back to rest.

order.rationale: That rumination lasts longer and recurs in depression is a clinical observation. No brain scan has followed a loop over hours, so its persistence here is assumed from behaviour, and the blunted reward response comes from separate studies of winning and losing.

regions.explanation: More active at rest during depression than in people who are not depressed, and more active in the depressed phase than after recovery in the same people. This rests on pooled findings of resting blood flow, but even this foundational finding has been challenged: without correcting for the region being smaller in depression, its activity can appear reduced. It is drawn at a steady raised level: the sources read do not say whether it rises further during rumination.
